title: Begging the Master to Pacify the Mind
author: Annotated by Zhiyu
excerpt: On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, a great snow fell. Guang stood firm and unmoving, and by dawn the snow had piled past his knees. The Patriarch, taking pity, asked: “You have stood long in the snow—what is it you seek?” Guang answered with tears: “I only wish that the Master, in his compassion, would open the gate of sweet dew and broadly deliver the host of beings.” The Patriarch said: “The unsurpassed wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort across kalpas without end—doing what is hard to do, enduring what cannot be endured.”

inline.s: (The original text is excerpted from the Compendium of the Five Lamps.)
On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, a great snow fell from the sky. Guang stood firm and unmoving, and by dawn the snow had piled past his knees
You have stood long in the snow—what is it you seek
Guang answered with tears of grief:
I only wish that the Master, in his compassion, would open the gate of sweet dew and broadly deliver the host of beings.
The unsurpassed wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort across kalpas without end—doing what is hard to do, enduring what cannot be endured
How could one of meager virtue and small wisdom, with a light heart and an arrogant mind, hope to attain the true vehicle
Such toil is all in vain!
Hearing the Patriarch’s admonition and encouragement, Guang secretly took a sharp knife, cut off his own left arm, and laid it before the Patriarch.

The Second Patriarch, Shenguang, came to Patriarch Bodhidharma to seek the Way, and day after day he stood respectfully outside the cave in attendance. On the night of the ninth day of the twelfth month of that year, a great snow fell, and Shenguang still stood firm and unmoving; by the time dawn drew near, the snow had piled past his knees. Taking pity, Bodhidharma asked: “You have stood long in the snow—what is it you seek?” Shenguang answered with tears of grief: “I only wish that the Master, in his compassion, would open the gate of sweet dew and broadly deliver the host of beings.” Bodhidharma said: “The unsurpassed wondrous Way of the Buddhas requires diligent effort across kalpas (long, distant kalpas) without end—doing what is hard to do, enduring what cannot be endured. How could one of meager virtue and small wisdom, with a light heart and an arrogant mind, hope to seek the true vehicle? Such toil is all in vain!” Hearing the Patriarch’s teaching and encouragement, Shenguang secretly took a sharp knife, cut off his own left arm, and laid it before the Patriarch.
[The gate of sweet dew] The unsurpassed wondrous Dharma that transcends birth and death and leads one into nirvana.

[The host of beings] All living beings. [The true vehicle] The true teaching. “Vehicle” uses raft and ferry, cart and carriage as metaphors for the teaching by which one crosses the sea of birth and death and reaches the other shore of nirvana.
The Patriarch knew he was a vessel of the Dharma, and so said:
When the Buddhas first sought the Way, for the Dharma’s sake they forgot their very bodies
Now that you have cut off your arm before me, you may well seek it
The Patriarch thereupon changed his name to Huike
May I hear the Dharma-seal of the Buddhas?
The Dharma-seal of the Buddhas is not obtained from another person
My mind is not yet at peace; I beg the Master to pacify it.
Bring your mind here, and I will pacify it for you.
After a long while Huike said:
I have searched for the mind and cannot find it at all.
I have pacified your mind for you.”
was a vessel of the Dharma,
: “When the Buddhas first sought the Way, for the Dharma’s sake they forgot their very
and it shows that you possess the sincere mind of one who forgets his very body for the Dharma’s sake in seeking the Way
cannot be attained merely by word of mouth and hearing
(it must be transmitted from mind to mind)
ke turned his light inward to search for that restless mind,
and after a long while (at which point the deluded mind had ceased and the true mind appeared) said
When I searched for that restless mind
—it is done (I have already pacified your mind for you)
[Vessel of the Dharma] One who possesses the capacity to cultivate and realize the Buddha-Dharma.

[Capacity] The root of a plant can grow branches, trunk, and leaves, and a vessel can hold things, yet what grows and what is held differ in size and amount; likewise, practitioners of the Way differ in ability, high and low, and so are compared to roots and vessels.
“Contemplate living beings, measure their capacities, and only then give to them.”
[The Dharma-seal] The Dharma by which the Buddhas and Patriarchs mutually confirm one another, transmitted from mind to mind, is therefore called the Dharma-seal.

When Huike turned his light inward to search for the mind, he at once entered a state in which not a single thought arose yet all was clear and distinct—the deluded mind ceased and the true mind appeared. He then answered:
“I have searched for the mind and cannot find it at all.”

(When he searched for that restless mind, it was nowhere to be found.) Seeing this, Bodhidharma knew that he had experienced the true mind and also knew how to extinguish the restless deluded mind, and so said in confirmation:
“I have pacified your mind—it is done
(your turning the light inward just now to search for that restless mind is itself the method of pacifying the mind)

was suddenly and greatly awakened: what he had just experienced was the wondrous method of pacifying the mind, and also the great method of practice. In the Sutra of Contemplating the Mind-ground of the Mahayana, the Buddha says:

is called the supreme secret Dharma-gate of the mind-ground of the Tathagatas of the ten directions; this Dharma is called the Dharma-gate of sudden awakening by which all ordinary beings enter the ground of the Tathagata; this Dharma is called the true and correct path by which all Bodhisattvas proceed toward great bodhi; this Dharma is called the subtle jeweled palace in which the Buddhas of the three times enjoy the bliss of the Dharma by themselves; this Dharma is called the inexhaustible treasure-store that benefits all sentient beings.
within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. One who can contemplate the mind attains ultimate liberation; one who cannot contemplate it remains forever in bondage.
[Confirmation] To certify what a disciple has attained and to praise and approve of it.
The Essentials of Cultivating the Mind says:
(the true mind in which not a single thought arises yet all is clear and distinct)
and guards it abides in the one-suchness, unmoving and liberated; one who is deluded about it and turns his back on it goes to the six paths
(For annotation see The Essentials of Cultivating the Mind, Fully Explained)

[Abiding in the one-suchness] “Abiding” means holding firmly. “One-suchness”: “one” means non-duality; “suchness” means non-difference. Non-dual and non-different is called “one-suchness.” “Abiding in the one-suchness” means holding firmly to the one-suchness.
Do you understand? If the mind is emptied, all pass the examination; the ordinary and the sage are from the first one and the same family.

[Passing the examination] In the era of the imperial examinations, being selected in the examinations. In particular, it refers to passing the jinshi examination; in the Ming and Qing dynasties it was used only for the top three of the palace examination. For example: “zhuangyuan jidi,” first place in the examination. Layman Pang said:
“This is the place for choosing Buddhas; when the mind is emptied, one passes and returns.”
[The ordinary and the sage are from the first one and the same family]
“When the self-nature is deluded, one is a living being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
(For details see The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, Fully Explained)
